title: America’s new gas boom | Wood Mackenzie
gist: An Energy Gang podcast episode debates whether the US gas industry can meet surging AI/data-centre power demand and rising LNG exports while preserving the low domestic price advantage. EQT CEO Toby Rice argues the shale resource base is deep enough to serve both markets without spiking prices, framing the goal as 'energy abundance'.

themes.theme: Gas demand drivers: AI and energy security

insights.claim: Surging electricity demand to power new data centres and growing energy-security fears from the Middle East conflict are putting US natural gas back at the center of the energy debate.
insights.speaker: Ed Crooks
insights.so_what: AI power demand plus geopolitics is a structural demand tailwind for US gas producers and infrastructure.
insights.quote: Surging demand for electricity to power new data centres, and growing fears about global energy security resulting from the conflict in the Middle East, are raising some urgent questions for the US gas industry.

insights.claim: US gas prices have been low by international standards for most of the past 20 years, and the central question is whether that advantage can persist against rising LNG exports and AI-driven power demand.
insights.speaker: Ed Crooks
insights.so_what: The cheap-gas advantage underpins US industrial competitiveness; its erosion is a macro risk to watch.
insights.quote: US gas prices have been low by international standards for most of the past 20 years. The big question is whether that price advantage can persist, in the face of rising LNG exports and growing power demand from AI.

insights.claim: Continued growth in gas demand could eventually push up domestic prices, weakening one of the US economy's biggest competitive advantages.
insights.speaker: Ed Crooks
insights.so_what: Higher domestic gas prices would raise input costs across US manufacturing and power.
insights.quote: Ed raises the prospect that continued growth in demand for gas could eventually push up domestic prices, weakening one of the US economy’s biggest competitive advantages.

insights.claim: Toby Rice argues America has the resources to meet rising domestic demand and supply much more gas to international markets without sending prices soaring.
insights.speaker: Toby Rice
insights.so_what: The bull case for US gas rests on abundant low-cost shale supply keeping prices in check even as demand climbs.
insights.quote: Toby argues that America has the resources both to meet rising domestic demand and to supply much more gas to international markets, without sending prices soaring.

insights.claim: Rice contends the shale resource base is deep enough that, at the right price signal, producers can bring on enough supply to serve both the domestic market and a much larger export system.
insights.speaker: Toby Rice
insights.so_what: Price-signal-driven supply elasticity is the key assumption keeping the low-price thesis intact.
insights.quote: He argues that at the right price signal, producers can bring on enough supply to support both the domestic market and a much larger export system.

insights.claim: Rice prefers to describe the administration's 'energy dominance' goal as 'energy abundance'.
insights.speaker: Toby Rice
insights.so_what: The 'abundance' framing signals a supply-maximising posture supportive of gas expansion policy.
insights.quote: The Trump administration often talks about “energy dominance”. Toby says. He prefers to describe the goal as “energy abundance”.

insights.claim: Rice argues increased US LNG export capacity strengthens American energy security by creating flexibility in times of stress, rather than simply exposing Americans to global volatility.
insights.speaker: Toby Rice
insights.so_what: Reframes LNG exports as a security asset, countering the price-exposure critique that could constrain export policy.
insights.quote: He also makes the case that increased US LNG export capacity can strengthen American energy security by creating more flexibility in times of stress, rather than simply exposing Americans to global volatility.

insights.claim: Amy Myers Jaffe questions whether energy-security anxiety after geopolitical shocks will make countries want more US LNG or instead accelerate investment in domestic alternatives like renewables, batteries, nuclear and coal.
insights.speaker: Amy Myers Jaffe
insights.so_what: Buyer substitution toward domestic alternatives is the key demand risk to the long-run US LNG export thesis.
insights.quote: will they still want more LNG, even if it comes from a reliable supplier such as the US? Or will they step up investment in domestic alternatives, including renewables, batteries, nuclear, and even coal?

themes.theme: Gas vs coal and emerging-market access

insights.claim: Rice makes the case for the environmental benefits of gas as a replacement for coal in power generation.
insights.speaker: Toby Rice
insights.so_what: Coal-to-gas switching is the emissions argument used to defend continued gas growth.
insights.quote: He also makes the case for the environmental benefits of gas as a replacement for coal in power generation.

insights.claim: Rice's nonprofit Energy Corps aims to deploy renewables, gas and propane for clean cooking to bring energy abundance and modern energy access to emerging markets.
insights.speaker: Toby Rice
insights.so_what: Signals producer positioning to expand gas/propane demand into underserved emerging markets.
insights.quote: It aims to deploy technologies including renewables, gas and propane for clean cooking, to increase access to modern energy
